## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

namingCustoms.content:
# Ireland Naming Customs

## Surnames

* Irish surnames of Gaelic origin were commonly used until England laid claim to Ireland in the fifteenth century. Legislation under English rule led to the anglicization of many Irish names and to the adoption of many English names. Many different forms of Irish surnames resulted. For example, the Irish surname Houlihan or O'Houlihan may have taken on the anglicized form Holland.
* Surname variations also resulted from an Irish form of patronymics that used the prefixes *Mac* (son of) and *O* (grandson or descendant of). These prefixes became fixed parts of hereditary surnames and were frequently dropped or restored over time, so the same family appears as O'Flynn, Flynn and Flinn across records.
* Spelling was not standardized; a single family's surname may be recorded several ways in one parish.

## Given Names

* Irish given names are also Gaelic in origin and were affected by the same English influences. As with surnames, many given names were anglicized, producing many given name variations. Darby, Dermot, and Jeremiah, for example, are all variations of the same name.
* Some given names are used for both males and females - Florence, Sydney, and Evelyn for example.
* Some given names have nicknames that little resemble the formal name.

### Traditional Naming Pattern

A traditional naming pattern was often used by Irish parents until the later 19th century:

* First son usually named for the father's father
* Second son usually named for the mother's father
* Third son usually named for the father
* Fourth son usually named for the father's eldest brother
* First daughter usually named for the mother's mother
* Second daughter usually named for the father's mother
* Third daughter usually named for the mother

The pattern is a clue, not a rule - it was not universally followed, and a broken pattern is not evidence of non-identity.

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

Here is the locality guide produced for **New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana, 1800–1830**:

---

**Survey findings** (logged as `loc_001` in the project):

**Notarial Records**
The primary confirmed digitized source for this period is a set of **notarial acts from 1803 to 1820**, available on FamilySearch but browseable only page-by-page — there is no name index. Records are in French and English. Original notarial acts — over 30 million pages dating from 1734 — are held at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**.

**Parish (Church) Registers**
The **Catholic sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral** (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the main church source; they run from 1731 with some gaps. The survey did not find them digitized on FamilySearch; researchers should check the **Archdiocese of New Orleans** and the **Louisiana State Archives** for access.

**Land Records**
Confirmed land records for Orleans Parish in this period were not identified in the survey. The **Bureau of Land Management (BLM) GLO Records** and the **Louisiana State Land Office** are the expected repositories for land patents and grants.

**Key Caveat — Fire Losses**
The **fires of 1788 and 1794** destroyed most colonial-era civil and church records, so coverage in the early years of this 1800–1830 window will be uneven.

**What was not confirmed by the survey:** Census, military, court, and immigration record series for Orleans Parish specifically in these years were not identified as digitized on FamilySearch — statewide Louisiana collections should be searched for Orleans-related entries.

**Recommended next step:** Search the browseable notarial volume and statewide Louisiana collections on FamilySearch, filtering for Orleans Parish entries.

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters
New Orleans suffered catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 that destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records. Despite these losses, significant genealogical sources survive for the early 1800s: sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, though with gaps), notarial records, and the records of the Cabildo (Spanish colonial governing body). The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]

## Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records
Louisiana's parish-based civil law system (unlike the county-based common law of other US states) means that many legal records are unique to Louisiana: successions (probate), tutorships (guardianship), and interdictions. The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System]

Then the offline sources.
- For notarial acts, the [New Orleans Genealogy wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) says the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages dating to 1734; those are the originals, and the FamilySearch volume is a microfilm copy.

Here is the locality guide produced for **Billy civil parish, County Antrim (Bushmills area), c. 1780–1870**:

---

## Locality Guide — Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, 1780–1870

### Church of Ireland Registers
The survey **could not confirm** that Church of Ireland registers for Billy parish are available in a digitized or easily searchable form. The FamilySearch wiki page for Billy does not list them, and no catalog hits were returned. To answer this definitively, the two authoritative sources to check are:

- **PRONI (Public Record Office of Northern Ireland)** — publishes a comprehensive guide to surviving church records for every Northern Ireland parish; many CoI registers are held there or microfilmed
- **Representative Church Body Library (Dublin)** — holds originals or microfilm for many Church of Ireland registers

### Civil Registration
| Event | Start date |
|---|---|
| Protestant marriages | 1845 |
| All births, deaths & marriages | 1864 |

Records from these dates are held at the **General Register Office (GRO)**, with indexes widely available on FamilySearch and elsewhere.

### Digitized FamilySearch Material Found
A small number of image volumes from the **Ballylinny area of Billy** were found, covering:
- **Christenings and marriages** from the late 1830s onward

These are browse-only (not indexed), so they require page-by-page searching.

There are also **valuation and school volumes** for the area that are browse-only on FamilySearch.

### Other Key Record Types for 1780–1870
Given County Antrim's record landscape, the following are typically the most valuable:

| Record type | Date range | Likely repository |
|---|---|---|
| Griffith's Valuation | c. 1847–1864 | PRONI; freely searchable at askaboutireland.ie |
| Tithe Applotment Books | 1823–1837 | PRONI; NAI; FamilySearch |
| Presbyterian session/baptism registers | varies | PRONI (many filmed) |
| Roman Catholic registers | varies | NLI; PRONI microfilm |
| Land surveys (estate papers) | 18th–19th c. | PRONI |
| Hearth Money Rolls | 1660s | useful for pre-1780 ancestry |

### Next Steps
1. **Check PRONI's online church records guide** for Billy's Church of Ireland parish registers — PRONI's eCatalogue (proni.gov.uk) lets you search by civil parish
2. **Check the Representative Church Body Library** register list if PRONI does not hold them
3. Use **Griffith's Valuation** (freely searchable) for mid-19th century landholders in Billy
4. Consult **Tithe Applotment** records for pre-1845 householder lists

> *Note: Church records availability for Billy could not be confirmed from tools in this session. PRONI and the RCB Library are the definitive authorities.*

[Northern Ireland](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Genealogy "Northern Ireland Genealogy")

Billy Civil Parish

Guide to **Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland ancestry, family history, and genealogy**. Parish registers, transcripts, baptism records, marriage records, and burial records.

## History

Billy is a parish, partly in the barony of Carey, but chiefly in that of Lower Dunluce, poor union of Coleraine, county of Antrim and province of Ulster; containing the post town of Bushmills and a portion of Dunserverick.

This parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union, that comprised also the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride, together forming the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor. The rectory and vicarage of Billy alone now constitute the corps of the archdeaconry. In the Roman Catholic divisions the parish forms part of the district of Coleraine. There are meeting houses for Presbyterians, for Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists.

## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

- **Alternative sources:** where registers are missing, the Billy page names no other sources. Use the general record-type rows (probate, land, newspapers) only after checking for the specific Billy records.
- **Finding aids:** the [Billy Civil Parish wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy) and the [Ireland Church Records page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records).

Here is the locality guide for **Billy civil parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)**:

---

## Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim — Locality Guide (1780–1870)

A survey of digitized church registers for Billy parish itself returned no results. The FamilySearch Research Wiki's Billy church sections are blank and do not identify which congregation(s) kept baptism and marriage registers for the parish during this period. The following repositories can fill that gap:

---

### Key Repositories

**Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)**
- **Address:** 2 Titanic Boulevard, Titanic Quarter, Belfast BT3 9HQ
- **Email:** proni@communities-ni.gov.uk
- **Phone:** 028 9053 4800
- **Why:** PRONI holds or indexes the surviving original church registers for County Antrim parishes. Its *Guide to Church Records* identifies which church served each civil parish and where its registers are held. The free reading room and enquiry service are the first stop for Billy parish coverage.

**Church of Ireland Representative Church Body (RCB) Library**
- **Address:** Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, D14 N735
- **Email:** library@ireland.anglican.org
- **Phone:** +353 1 492 3979
- **Why:** Holds Church of Ireland registers not transferred to PRONI. Offers a paid request-a-search service for researchers who cannot visit in person.

---

### Online Indexes

| Site | URL | Notes |
|------|-----|-------|
| **RootsIreland** | rootsireland.ie | Paid index of transcribed church records (baptism, marriage, burial) for many Irish parishes, including Ulster. Search here to identify surviving register entries for Billy. |
| **IrishGenealogy.ie** | irishgenealogy.ie | Free government index — does **not** cover County Antrim; not useful here. |
| **PRONI Online** | nidirect.gov.uk/proni | Catalogue and some digitized records; use to identify Billy's church register references before visiting. |
| **FamilySearch** | familysearch.org | Search "Ireland, County Antrim" collections; some Ulster registers are microfilmed. |

---

### A Note on Coverage

Two volumes surfaced in the search with the name **Ballylinny** — the FamilySearch Wiki treats Ballylinny as a *separate* civil parish, so those registers should not be assumed to cover Billy.

**Recommended next step:** Contact PRONI to confirm which church(es) served Billy civil parish and whether their registers survive, before planning further searches.

Billy Civil Parish

Guide to **Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland ancestry, family history, and genealogy**. Parish registers, transcripts, baptism records, marriage records, and burial records.

## History

Billy is a parish, partly in the barony of Carey, but chiefly in that of Lower Dunluce, poor union of Coleraine, county of Antrim and province of Ulster; containing the post town of Bushmills and a portion of Dunserverick.

This parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union, that comprised also the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride, together forming the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor. The rectory and vicarage of Billy alone now constitute the corps of the archdeaconry. In the Roman Catholic divisions the parish forms part of the district of Coleraine. There are meeting houses for Presbyterians, for Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists.

getting_started.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

## Ballylinny Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland Genealogy — Church records

### Cemeteries  
The townland of Ballylinny has two graveyards one is Presbyterian the other is not stated.

### Church records  
#### Catholic  
The Roman Catholics living in the civil parish have a meeting place in Ballyclare. The parish is part of Ballyclare and part of Carrickfergus in the diocese of Connor. Ballyclare's earliest register for baptisms is July 1869 and for marriages February 1870. The records have been indexed by the Ulster Historical Foundation.  
#### Church of Ireland  
As stated above the church was destroyed in Ballylinny, parishioners meet at the Carnmoney parish church. The registers in Carnmoney begin as follows: baptisms: 1788; marriages 1789; deaths: 1845.  
#### Presbyterian  
The Presbyterian population in Ballylinny attended church in Ballyclare and church registers begin for both baptisms and marriages in 1837. The original register are in the custody of the local church. Microfilm copies of these records can be found at the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI) film number MIC 1P/327 (1851-); FamilySearch Library film number 973220 (cover baptisms/marriages from 1837).

args.guideSection:
## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Billy is a civil parish partly in the barony of Carey and chiefly in Lower Dunluce, in the Coleraine poor union, county of Antrim, province of Ulster; it contains the post town of Bushmills and part of Dunserverick ([Billy Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)). The formation date is not stated.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.
- **Population during period:** Not returned by the survey (population lookup: none found).
- **Economy:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Religious denominations:** Presbyterian, Covenanter and Wesleyan Methodist meeting houses; Roman Catholic district of Coleraine ([Billy Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)).
- **Key historical events:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Coverage of this survey:** The Billy-level volume search returned 4 volumes, all 4 listed. Two of them are filed under Ballylinny and one is a school volume. The survey returned no collections and no Catalog hits.

args.guideSection:
## Boundary changes
- The survey found no boundary change in its tool results. The jurisdiction's date range in FamilySearch's place standard is "/+1922" for the Ireland form and "+1922/" for the Northern Ireland form, which the place search returned without explanation.
- Billy is a civil parish. Its ecclesiastical history: it was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union with Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore and Kilbride, and now alone forms the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor ([Billy Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)). Church records may therefore sit with the union's parishes or with the archdeaconry, not only with Billy.
- Ballylinny, which the volumes are filed under, is treated by the wiki as its own civil parish, not a part of Billy ([Ballylinny Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ballylinny_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)).

args.guideSection:
## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the PRONI Guide to Church Records (free, [nidirect.gov.uk](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf)) to identify which church served Billy and whether its registers are in PRONI on microfilm or as originals. Next, check the PRONI list of digitised church records, then the Church of Ireland RCB Library's list of parish registers. RootsIreland is a paid index and should come after you know which register to look for. The Billy volumes (Ballylinny christenings and marriages, full-text searchable) are for Ballylinny, so do not search them as Billy's registers until a source confirms the parish.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's Ireland Church Records page lists PRONI as holding digitised and microfilmed church records, and points to its [Digitised Church Records Available in PRONI](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1) list ([Ireland Church Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)).
- For Church of Ireland registers, the RCB Library offers a paid request-a-search service and publishes a [List of Parish Registers](https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf) ([Ireland Church Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)).
- For Presbyterian registers, the Ballylinny page shows that a congregation's original registers may stay with the local church, with microfilm at PRONI and FamilySearch. Billy's Presbyterian congregation is not named by any tool result, so ask PRONI which congregation Billy's Presbyterians used ([Ballylinny Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ballylinny_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records)).
- Civil registration of births and deaths began in 1864 and Protestant marriages in 1845, per the [Billy Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy). The wiki does not state the level, so do not assume a parish-level or statewide series.
- Griffith's valuation (1840s) and Tithe Applotments (1820s) are the tax lists the Billy page names; see the [Ireland Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Land_and_Property) page for detail, which this survey did not read.
- Do not use IrishGenealogy.ie for Billy: the Ireland Church Records page lists its coverage as Kerry, western and northwestern Cork, and most of Dublin ([Ireland Church Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)).
- Alternative sources when the registers are missing: the Billy page's tax and civil-registration links, and the Ballylinny graveyards for cemetery leads, though those are for Ballylinny.

loc_001 saved for Billy, County Antrim.

---

Billy parish in County Antrim, Northern Ireland, was surveyed for 1780 to 1870, and no digitized church register for Billy itself turned up. The FamilySearch Wiki's Billy church sections are blank, so it does not say which church kept Billy's baptisms and marriages. The best places to close that gap are the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI), at 2 Titanic Boulevard, Titanic Quarter, Belfast BT3 9HQ (enquiries at proni@communities-ni.gov.uk or 028 9053 4800; its free enquiry service and its Guide to Church Records show which church served a parish and where its registers are), and the Church of Ireland RCB Library, at Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, D14 N735 (library@ireland.anglican.org or +353 1 492 3979; it runs a paid request-a-search service). RootsIreland (rootsireland.ie) is a paid index, not the original registers, and IrishGenealogy.ie does not cover County Antrim. Two of the four volumes the search returned are labelled Ballylinny, which the Wiki treats as a separate civil parish, so they should not be read as Billy registers.

Next, research-plan can use this guide to plan the church-register search, starting with identifying which church served Billy.

# Locality Guide: Billy, County Antrim, Ireland (1780-1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Billy is a civil parish partly in the barony of Carey and chiefly in Lower Dunluce, in the Coleraine poor union, county of Antrim, province of Ulster; it contains the post town of Bushmills and part of Dunserverick ([Billy Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)). The formation date is not stated.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.
- **Population during period:** Not returned by the survey (population lookup: none found).
- **Economy:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Religious denominations:** Presbyterian, Covenanter and Wesleyan Methodist meeting houses; Roman Catholic district of Coleraine ([Billy Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)).
- **Key historical events:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Coverage of this survey:** The Billy-level volume search returned 4 volumes, all 4 listed. Two of them are filed under Ballylinny and one is a school volume. The survey returned no collections and no Catalog hits.

## Boundary changes
- The survey found no boundary change in its tool results. The jurisdiction's date range in FamilySearch's place standard is "/+1922" for the Ireland form and "+1922/" for the Northern Ireland form, which the place search returned without explanation.
- Billy is a civil parish. Its ecclesiastical history: it was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union with Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore and Kilbride, and now alone forms the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor ([Billy Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)). Church records may therefore sit with the union's parishes or with the archdeaconry, not only with Billy.
- Ballylinny, which the volumes are filed under, is treated by the wiki as its own civil parish, not a part of Billy ([Ballylinny Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ballylinny_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)).

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the PRONI Guide to Church Records (free, [nidirect.gov.uk](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf)) to identify which church served Billy and whether its registers are in PRONI on microfilm or as originals. Next, check the PRONI list of digitised church records, then the Church of Ireland RCB Library's list of parish registers. RootsIreland is a paid index and should come after you know which register to look for. The Billy volumes (Ballylinny christenings and marriages, full-text searchable) are for Ballylinny, so do not search them as Billy's registers until a source confirms the parish.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's Ireland Church Records page lists PRONI as holding digitised and microfilmed church records, and points to its [Digitised Church Records Available in PRONI](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1) list ([Ireland Church Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)).
- For Church of Ireland registers, the RCB Library offers a paid request-a-search service and publishes a [List of Parish Registers](https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf) ([Ireland Church Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)).
- For Presbyterian registers, the Ballylinny page shows that a congregation's original registers may stay with the local church, with microfilm at PRONI and FamilySearch. Billy's Presbyterian congregation is not named by any tool result, so ask PRONI which congregation Billy's Presbyterians used ([Ballylinny Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ballylinny_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records)).
- Civil registration of births and deaths began in 1864 and Protestant marriages in 1845, per the [Billy Civil Parish wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy). The wiki does not state the level, so do not assume a parish-level or statewide series.
- Griffith's valuation (1840s) and Tithe Applotments (1820s) are the tax lists the Billy page names; see the [Ireland Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Land_and_Property) page for detail, which this survey did not read.
- Do not use IrishGenealogy.ie for Billy: the Ireland Church Records page lists its coverage as Kerry, western and northwestern Cork, and most of Dublin ([Ireland Church Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)).
- Alternative sources when the registers are missing: the Billy page's tax and civil-registration links, and the Ballylinny graveyards for cemetery leads, though those are for Ballylinny.

Here is what the locality-guide subagent found for **Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1840s–1860s**:

---

### Record Availability — Schuylkill County, PA (1840–1869)

**What was found:**

- **1850 U.S. Federal Census** — largely name-searchable; a strong starting point.
- **Probate Records (1845–1880)** — searchable by full text, though only lightly indexed by name.
- **Lutheran Church Register (1840–1875)** — partly in German; can only be browsed page by page (no name index). This is significant for a heavily German-immigrant county.

**Notable gaps:**

- **No civil vital records** (birth, marriage, death registration) for this period — Pennsylvania did not require civil registration until 1885, so this is expected.
- The catalog search returned no additional hits, which likely reflects incomplete cataloguing rather than a true absence of other records.

**Caution:** One collection in the results is flagged as a synthetic test fixture and should be verified before relying on it.

---

**Research implications for the 1840s–1860s in Schuylkill County:**
- The 1850 (and 1860) census should be the first search.
- Church registers — especially Lutheran and Catholic, given the immigrant mining community — are essential substitutes for absent civil records.
- Probate records are available via full-text search and may surface family members as heirs or witnesses.
- For marriages and baptisms, browsing unindexed church register images will likely be necessary.

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

[Kentucky](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy "Kentucky, United States Genealogy")

Pulaski County

Guide to **Pulaski County, Kentucky ancestry, genealogy and family history**, birth records, marriage records, death records, census records, and military records.

### County Courthouse

**Pulaski County Courthouse**  
100 N. Main Street, #208  
Somerset, KY 42502  
Phone: 606-679-3652[[3]](#cite_note-3)

### Pulaski County, Kentucky Record Dates

Information for this chart was taken from various sources, often containing conflicting dates. This information should be taken as a guide and should be verified by contacting the county and/or the state government agency.

**Known Beginning Dates for Government County Records**[[4]](#cite_note-4)

| Records | [Birth*](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy#Birth "Pulaski County, Kentucky Genealogy") | [Marriage](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy#Marriage "Pulaski County, Kentucky Genealogy") | [Death*](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy#Death "Pulaski County, Kentucky Genealogy") | [Court](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy#Court_Records "Pulaski County, Kentucky Genealogy") | [Land](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy#Land_and_Property_Records "Pulaski County, Kentucky Genealogy") | [Probate](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy#Probate_Records "Pulaski County, Kentucky Genealogy") | [Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy#Census_Records "Pulaski County, Kentucky Genealogy") |

### Record Loss

|  |
| --- |
| **1838, 1871--**A disaster destroyed some records.   For suggestions about research in places that suffered historic record losses, see:   * [*Burned Counties.*](http://blogs.ancestry.com/circle/?p=2424) By Michael John Neill at [24-7 Family History Circle](https://blogs.ancestry.com/circle/). * [*When the Records are Gone.*](http://tnblog.arleneeakle.com/2009/04/13/when-the-records-are-gone/) By Arlene Eakle at [Arlene Eakle's Tennessee Blog](http://tnblog.arleneeakle.com/). * [Burned Counties Research](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Burned_Counties_Research "Burned Counties Research") in the [FamilySearch Research Wiki.](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Main_Page "Main Page") * [List of counties in the United States with Record Loss](https://user.xmission.com/~jsvare/record_coverage/US_County_Records_Loss.html) |

### Boundary Changes

|  |
| --- |
| * **1798**--Pulaski County was created 10 December 1798 from [Lincoln](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Lincoln_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy "Lincoln County, Kentucky Genealogy") and [Green](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Green_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy "Green County, Kentucky Genealogy") Counties. * **County seat:** Somerset[[5]](#cite_note-5) * [Kentucky Individual County Chronologies](https://digital.newberry.org/ahcb/documents/KY_Individual_County_Chronologies.htm#Individual_County_Chronologies) - Newberry Library list of all boundary changes by county * [Kentucky Historical Borders - Map](https://publications.newberry.org/ahcb/map/map.html#KY) at Newberry Library Atlas of Historical County Boundaries; *Also at:* [mapofus.org](http://www.mapofus.org/kentucky/) - animated maps illustrating Kentucky county boundary changes |

### History Timeline

* 1800, May - "First landing, for loading and unloading merchandise shipped by flatboats on the Cumberland River, was the James Montgomery landing."[[7]](#cite_note-7)
* 1802 - Road from Somerset (Pulaski County) to Danville (Lincoln County) started.
* 1812 - By 1812 Goose Creek Salt Works was in existence, along with a road from Somerset to it that passed over a bridge at Flat Lick.[[8]](#cite_note-8)
* 1818 - Road from Somerset to the Mount Vernon viewed. (Intersecting a road named Tall Works, in direction of Henry James mill, and passing by Hughes mill.)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

# Kentucky Vital Records

[U.S. Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Vital_Records "United States Vital Records")

[Kentucky](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy "Kentucky, United States Genealogy")

Vital Records

## Kentucky Vital Records Dates

Years Vital Records Started in Kentucky

| **Government Registration** | **[Births](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Birth_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Marriages](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Marriage_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Deaths](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Death_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **County/Town** | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 | County Formation | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 |
| **Statewide Registration** | 1911 | 1958 | 1911 |
| **General Compliance** | 1917 | County Formation | 1917 |

## Background

Kentucky's vital registration history is complicated by several periods of partial compliance. Between 1852 and 1862, registration was assigned to county tax assessors who recorded events submitted by clergy, midwives, or doctors in attendance, as well as the head of household. Compliance with the law was minimal, and records were often incomplete or inaccurate. The law lapsed in 1862 during the Civil War, was briefly revived from 1874 to 1878, and again from 1892 to 1910 with poor compliance. Statewide registration began in 1911, with high compliance achieved by about 1917.

## Access Restrictions

Birth records are restricted for 100 years after the date of the event. Death records are restricted for 50 years. Marriage records are public.

## Primary Repositories

- **Kentucky Department of Public Health, Office of Vital Statistics** — statewide records from 1911 to the present
- **Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA)** — pre-1911 county-level records
- **Individual county courthouses** — marriage bonds and licenses from county formation; scattered early birth and death records

churchRecords.content:
# Kentucky Church Records

## Background

Before 1900 the largest religious groups in Kentucky were the Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian churches. Church records can predate civil registration and may be the only record of baptisms, marriages, and burials for early settlers.

## Record Types

Church records may contain:
- Baptisms or christenings
- Marriage records
- Funerals or burials
- Membership lists
- Minutes or historical narratives

## Online Resources

### FamilySearch Collections
- **Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995** — index and images (incomplete)
- **Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960** — index only
- **Kentucky Marriages, 1785–1979** — index only
- **Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970** — index only

## Catholic Diocese Coverage

Kentucky is divided among four Roman Catholic dioceses: Covington, Lexington, Louisville, and Owensboro. Each diocese maintains parish-level sacramental records (baptism, marriage, burial). County assignments for each diocese are documented on the wiki.

## Research Strategies

1. Search online digitized records at FamilySearch and Ancestry
2. Search the FamilySearch Library catalog for microfilmed church records
3. Contact the denominational archive for the relevant church body
4. Contact historical and genealogical societies in the county
5. Contact the active congregation directly — many smaller churches still hold their own records

## Key Repositories

- **FamilySearch Library** — microfilmed church records from many Kentucky congregations
- **Kentucky Historical Society** — Frankfort; manuscript church records
- **Filson Historical Society** — Louisville; holds Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian records for the Louisville area
- **Individual denominational archives** — Baptist (Southern Baptist Historical Library, Nashville), Methodist (various conference archives), Presbyterian (Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia)

# Kentucky Vital Records

[U.S. Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Vital_Records "United States Vital Records")

[Kentucky](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy "Kentucky, United States Genealogy")

Vital Records

## Kentucky Vital Records Dates

Years Vital Records Started in Kentucky

| **Government Registration** | **[Births](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Birth_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Marriages](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Marriage_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Deaths](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Death_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **County/Town** | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 | County Formation | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 |
| **Statewide Registration** | 1911 | 1958 | 1911 |
| **General Compliance** | 1917 | County Formation | 1917 |

## Background

Kentucky's vital registration history is complicated by several periods of partial compliance. Between 1852 and 1862, registration was assigned to county tax assessors who recorded events submitted by clergy, midwives, or doctors in attendance, as well as the head of household. Compliance with the law was minimal, and records were often incomplete or inaccurate. The law lapsed in 1862 during the Civil War, was briefly revived from 1874 to 1878, and again from 1892 to 1910 with poor compliance. Statewide registration began in 1911, with high compliance achieved by about 1917.

## Access Restrictions

Birth records are restricted for 100 years after the date of the event. Death records are restricted for 50 years. Marriage records are public.

## Primary Repositories

- **Kentucky Department of Public Health, Office of Vital Statistics** — statewide records from 1911 to the present
- **Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA)** — pre-1911 county-level records
- **Individual county courthouses** — marriage bonds and licenses from county formation; scattered early birth and death records

churchRecords.content:
# Kentucky Church Records

## Background

Before 1900 the largest religious groups in Kentucky were the Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian churches. Church records can predate civil registration and may be the only record of baptisms, marriages, and burials for early settlers.

## Record Types

Church records may contain:
- Baptisms or christenings
- Marriage records
- Funerals or burials
- Membership lists
- Minutes or historical narratives

## Online Resources

### FamilySearch Collections
- **Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995** — index and images (incomplete)
- **Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960** — index only
- **Kentucky Marriages, 1785–1979** — index only
- **Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970** — index only

## Catholic Diocese Coverage

Kentucky is divided among four Roman Catholic dioceses: Covington, Lexington, Louisville, and Owensboro. Each diocese maintains parish-level sacramental records (baptism, marriage, burial). County assignments for each diocese are documented on the wiki.

## Research Strategies

1. Search online digitized records at FamilySearch and Ancestry
2. Search the FamilySearch Library catalog for microfilmed church records
3. Contact the denominational archive for the relevant church body
4. Contact historical and genealogical societies in the county
5. Contact the active congregation directly — many smaller churches still hold their own records

## Key Repositories

- **FamilySearch Library** — microfilmed church records from many Kentucky congregations
- **Kentucky Historical Society** — Frankfort; manuscript church records
- **Filson Historical Society** — Louisville; holds Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian records for the Louisville area
- **Individual denominational archives** — Baptist (Southern Baptist Historical Library, Nashville), Methodist (various conference archives), Presbyterian (Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia)

getting_started.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

# Kentucky Vital Records

[U.S. Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Vital_Records "United States Vital Records")

[Kentucky](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky,_United_States_Genealogy "Kentucky, United States Genealogy")

Vital Records

## Kentucky Vital Records Dates

Years Vital Records Started in Kentucky

| **Government Registration** | **[Births](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Birth_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Marriages](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Marriage_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** | **[Deaths](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records#Death_Records "Kentucky Vital Records")** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **County/Town** | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 | County Formation | 1853-1862, 1874-1878, 1892-1910 |
| **Statewide Registration** | 1911 | 1958 | 1911 |
| **General Compliance** | 1917 | County Formation | 1917 |

## Background

Kentucky's vital registration history is complicated by several periods of partial compliance. Between 1852 and 1862, registration was assigned to county tax assessors who recorded events submitted by clergy, midwives, or doctors in attendance, as well as the head of household. Compliance with the law was minimal, and records were often incomplete or inaccurate. The law lapsed in 1862 during the Civil War, was briefly revived from 1874 to 1878, and again from 1892 to 1910 with poor compliance. Statewide registration began in 1911, with high compliance achieved by about 1917.

## Access Restrictions

Birth records are restricted for 100 years after the date of the event. Death records are restricted for 50 years. Marriage records are public.

## Primary Repositories

- **Kentucky Department of Public Health, Office of Vital Statistics** — statewide records from 1911 to the present
- **Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA)** — pre-1911 county-level records
- **Individual county courthouses** — marriage bonds and licenses from county formation; scattered early birth and death records

churchRecords.content:
# Kentucky Church Records

## Background

Before 1900 the largest religious groups in Kentucky were the Baptist, Methodist, Roman Catholic, and Presbyterian churches. Church records can predate civil registration and may be the only record of baptisms, marriages, and burials for early settlers.

## Record Types

Church records may contain:
- Baptisms or christenings
- Marriage records
- Funerals or burials
- Membership lists
- Minutes or historical narratives

## Online Resources

### FamilySearch Collections
- **Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995** — index and images (incomplete)
- **Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960** — index only
- **Kentucky Marriages, 1785–1979** — index only
- **Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970** — index only

## Catholic Diocese Coverage

Kentucky is divided among four Roman Catholic dioceses: Covington, Lexington, Louisville, and Owensboro. Each diocese maintains parish-level sacramental records (baptism, marriage, burial). County assignments for each diocese are documented on the wiki.

## Research Strategies

1. Search online digitized records at FamilySearch and Ancestry
2. Search the FamilySearch Library catalog for microfilmed church records
3. Contact the denominational archive for the relevant church body
4. Contact historical and genealogical societies in the county
5. Contact the active congregation directly — many smaller churches still hold their own records

## Key Repositories

- **FamilySearch Library** — microfilmed church records from many Kentucky congregations
- **Kentucky Historical Society** — Frankfort; manuscript church records
- **Filson Historical Society** — Louisville; holds Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian records for the Louisville area
- **Individual denominational archives** — Baptist (Southern Baptist Historical Library, Nashville), Methodist (various conference archives), Presbyterian (Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia)

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

research_tips.content:
## Pennsylvania Research Strategies

### Starting Points
Begin with FamilySearch's Pennsylvania collections, which include census, probate, church, and vital records. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds county deed and probate originals not fully digitized. County courthouse records (deeds, wills, orphans' court) survive well from the late 1700s onward.

### Church Records
Pennsylvania's diverse religious heritage means church records are often the best pre-1906 vital record substitute. Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic, Quaker, and Mennonite congregations kept registers from the colonial period. The Diocese of Philadelphia (1808) split into Harrisburg (1868), Scranton (1868), and Pittsburgh (1843) dioceses; match the county to the diocese for Catholic records. German-language church records (Kirchenbücher) require German paleography skills.

### Vital Records
Statewide civil registration began in 1906 (death certificates) and 1913 (birth/marriage certificates). Before 1906, rely on church registers, county court marriage bonds (available in many counties from the 1790s), and cemetery records.

### Census
Pennsylvania is covered in every federal census 1790–1940. The 1890 census is largely destroyed; bridge with 1880 and 1900. The 1880 census introduces the relationship-to-head column, enabling direct family reconstruction. Pennsylvania also conducted state censuses in 1779 and 1784.

### Naturalization
Early naturalizations (pre-1906) occurred in any court of record — county courts, not just federal court. Search county prothonotary records and Quarter Sessions minutes. Post-1906 naturalizations centralized in federal courts; NARA Philadelphia holds local district court records.

### Probate and Land
County Orphans' Courts handled probate; records survive from the 1700s in most counties and are strong for identifying heirs and family relationships. Deed books at county courthouses provide migration evidence — look for grantors selling property before moves.

churchRecords.content:
## Pennsylvania Church Records

Pennsylvania has significant church records for many denominations dating to the colonial period. Records are held across denominational archives, diocesan repositories, individual congregations, and the FamilySearch Library.

### Episcopal/Anglican Records

For parishes that remain active, contact the church directly for access to its original registers. The **Diocese of Pennsylvania** holds records for closed Episcopal churches in Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, and Philadelphia counties. The Diocese of Bethlehem holds records for closed parishes in 14 counties north and west of Philadelphia. The Diocese of Central Pennsylvania holds records for closed parishes in its territory.

### Historical Society of Pennsylvania

The Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) in Philadelphia holds four FamilySearch-indexed collections:
- **Pennsylvania, HSP, Congregational Records (1620–1991)**
- **Pennsylvania, HSP, Births and Baptisms (1520–1999)**
- **Pennsylvania, HSP, Marriages (1512–1989)**
- **Pennsylvania, HSP, Deaths and Burials (1856–1971)**

These collections are described as abstracts **taken from various Pennsylvania Church Records**.

### Lutheran Archives

The **Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia** holds records for closed parishes in most Pennsylvania synods. The Tri-Synod Archives at Thiel College (Greenville) covers the former Pittsburgh, Allegheny, and Wartburg synods. The A.R. Wentz Library at United Lutheran Seminary holds records for Central Pennsylvania (restricted; the FamilySearch Library has microfilm copies).

### Presbyterian Historical Society

The **Presbyterian Historical Society** in Philadelphia holds original records for Pennsylvania Presbyterian congregations.

### Mennonite and Moravian Records

The **Mennonite Heritage Center** (Harleysville) holds Mennonite congregational records. The **Northern Province Moravian Archives** (Bethlehem) holds Moravian records for Pennsylvania congregations.

### Evangelical and Reformed Historical Society

The **Evangelical and Reformed Historical Society** (Lancaster Theological Seminary, Lancaster) holds records for Reformed and Evangelical congregations. Some holdings are original documents; others are photocopies, digitized scans, or transcriptions.

### FamilySearch Library

Microfilm copies of many Pennsylvania church records are held at the FamilySearch Library in Salt Lake City and may be ordered through local FamilySearch Centers.

The locality guide for the Alabama region circa 1800 has been saved (loc_001). Here is what the survey found:

---

**Alabama Region, c. 1800 — Records Context**

Around 1800, the land that would become Alabama was organized as the **Mississippi Territory** (1798–1817), then the **Alabama Territory** until statehood in 1819. Records are filed under those territorial names, not "Alabama."

**Key repositories and records:**

- **Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery)** — Holds territorial censuses for **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810**, plus territorial land and court records (some are browse-only page images with no name index).
- **Mobile-area records** (French and Spanish colonial period) — Held in overseas/foreign archives; some microfilm is available in Mobile.
- **FamilySearch catalog** — The catalog search returned no hits for this period, which likely reflects a cataloging gap rather than a true absence of records.

**What is not confirmed for this period:** vital records, probate, newspapers, and cemetery records. These either don't survive or weren't captured in the survey's sources for this era.

---

**Next step:** If you share the county or district within the territory where your ancestor lived, a research plan can be built starting with the territorial census and land collections.

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records
Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory from 1798 to 1817, then became the Alabama Territory until statehood in 1819. Territorial records include land grants, tax lists, militia rolls, and court records. The earliest land records are Spanish and British colonial grants in the Mobile area. The Mississippi Territory census of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These territorial censuses are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records]

## Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records
Before American control, the Mobile area was administered by France (1702-1763), Britain (1763-1780), and Spain (1780-1813). French colonial records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence and in microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish records of the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records]

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama had no separate jurisdiction around 1800. The area was part of the Mississippi Territory from 1798 to 1817, then Alabama Territory until statehood in 1819 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory, United States (1798/1817).
- **Population during period:** The survey returned no population figures. The territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808 and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Economy:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** Not confirmed by this survey. Spanish and British colonial rule in the Mobile area is noted (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Religious denominations:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Key historical events:** Colonial administration of the Mobile area passed from France (1702-1763) to Britain (1763-1780) to Spain (1780-1813) (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Coverage of this survey:** The Mississippi Territory level lists 1 digitized volume and 4 collections; the Catalog returned 0 hits.

args.guideSection:
## Boundary changes
- The Mississippi Territory covered the area from 1798 to 1817 (+1798/1817 per the place record).

Here is the locality guide returned for Arkansas before 1800:

---

**Locality Guide: Arkansas (pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Period)**
*Saved as loc_001 in the project.*

Records for this period are sparse and center almost entirely on **Arkansas Post** — the French settlement founded in 1686 and placed under Spanish authority from 1763 to 1800. Here is what survives and where:

### Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) | Spanish-era civil and military records, land grants, colonial papers |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Spanish-era church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) for Arkansas Post |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Colonial administrative records for Spanish Louisiana, including Arkansas Post |
| **Library of Congress** | Microfilm of some Spanish colonial records |

### Key Record Set
The only digitized pre-1800 item identified is a **Spanish-language register volume covering 1763–1800** for Arkansas Post. It is **not indexed** — it must be browsed image by image and read in Spanish.

### Important Caveats
- Every indexed FamilySearch collection for Arkansas begins **1819 or later** and will not cover this period.
- Research in this era requires **Spanish-language paleography skills** and familiarity with Catholic sacramental record conventions.
- The Archivo General de Indias in Seville holds the deepest colonial administrative record and may require a specialist or remote research service.

### Suggested Next Step
Given the specialized nature of this period (pre-statehood Spanish colonial Arkansas), consider whether this warrants its own dedicated research project before working through the Arkansas Post registers.

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

## Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records
Arkansas Post, established in 1686, was the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley. Under Spanish administration (1763-1800), civil and military records were kept at the post, including censuses (padrones), baptismal and marriage registers, and land concessions. French Catholic missionaries maintained sacramental registers at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s. These registers record baptisms, marriages, and burials of both European settlers and Native Americans. Surviving registers are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and in transcribed form at the Arkansas History Commission.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records]

## Ohio, United States Genealogy — Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes
Ohio was created from the Northwest Territory, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Before statehood in 1803, the region underwent several jurisdictional changes: Washington County (1788) was the first county organized, followed by Hamilton County (1790). Boundary changes were frequent — researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event. Early court and land records are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio,_United_States_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory]

## Ohio, United States Genealogy — Land Records
The Virginia Military District (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers) was reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans and used a metes-and-bounds survey system. The Connecticut Western Reserve in northeastern Ohio was surveyed on a different grid. Each district has its own land-grant records: Virginia Military District warrants are at the Virginia State Library; Connecticut Western Reserve records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio,_United_States_Genealogy#Land_Records]

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

## Ohio, United States Genealogy — Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes
Ohio was created from the Northwest Territory, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Before statehood in 1803, the region underwent several jurisdictional changes: Washington County (1788) was the first county organized, followed by Hamilton County (1790). Boundary changes were frequent — researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event. Early court and land records are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio,_United_States_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory]

## Ohio, United States Genealogy — Land Records
The Virginia Military District (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers) was reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans and used a metes-and-bounds survey system. The Connecticut Western Reserve in northeastern Ohio was surveyed on a different grid. Each district has its own land-grant records: Virginia Military District warrants are at the Virginia State Library; Connecticut Western Reserve records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio,_United_States_Genealogy#Land_Records]

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).
