## Ohio, United States Genealogy — Northwest Territory and Boundary Changes
Ohio was created from the Northwest Territory, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Before statehood in 1803, the region underwent several jurisdictional changes: Washington County (1788) was the first county organized, followed by Hamilton County (1790). Boundary changes were frequent — researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event. Early court and land records are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio,_United_States_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory]

## Ohio, United States Genealogy — Land Records
The Virginia Military District (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers) was reserved for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans and used a metes-and-bounds survey system. The Connecticut Western Reserve in northeastern Ohio was surveyed on a different grid. Each district has its own land-grant records: Virginia Military District warrants are at the Virginia State Library; Connecticut Western Reserve records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio,_United_States_Genealogy#Land_Records]

# Locality Guide: Ohio country before statehood (Northwest Territory, c. 1790) (1787-1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Ohio was created from the Northwest Territory, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787; statehood came in 1803 (place_search dateRange "+1803/").
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not returned by any tool result.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory (no standard place resolved by place_search_all).
- **Population during period:** The population lookup returned "none found".

- **Ethnic composition:** Not returned by any tool result.
- **Religious denominations:** Not returned by any tool result beyond the collection title Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950.
- **Key historical events:** Not returned by any tool result.
- **Coverage of this survey:** Catalog lookups returned 0 hits; the survey did not return a count of volumes beyond the two listed.

## Boundary changes
- The Northwest Territory (1787) was the governing unit before statehood in 1803.
- Washington County (1788) was the first county organized, followed by Hamilton County (1790). Per the FamilySearch Wiki, boundary changes were frequent and researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event ([Ohio, United States Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio,_United_States_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)).
- The Virginia Military District and the Connecticut Western Reserve were separate survey districts with their own land records (see [Land Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio,_United_States_Genealogy#Land_Records)).
- No tool result stated the exact boundary of each county in 1790; this survey does not settle which county held a given event.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840 collection (1542187) and the Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950 collection (2246917), since both are indexed collections that reach back to the territorial period. Then check the Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850 collection (1987542) for the years after 1800. Browse the Territorial Land Records image group (005112233, 51 images, 0% name-searchable) by hand.
- The Ohio History Connection in Columbus holds early court and land records, per the [Ohio, United States Genealogy page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio,_United_States_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory).
- For Virginia Military District warrants, the survey names the Virginia State Library; for Connecticut Western Reserve records, the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland ([Land Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio,_United_States_Genealogy#Land_Records)).
- Catalog lookups returned no hits, so this is a cataloguing gap, not evidence that records are missing.
- The generic wiki home page says federal census records begin in 1790 with gaps, and state or territorial censuses may fill them; this survey did not confirm any Ohio-specific early census ([Genealogy Research Guide](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide)).
- Neighbouring jurisdictions were not listed by any tool result; check adjoining areas across the Ohio River and the Pennsylvania border as the family's known locations suggest.
- Pre-1803 Ohio records were filed under the Northwest Territory and its counties, so search both the county of residence and any county later carved from it.

---

**California Locality Guide — Gold Rush Era (1850s)**

California became a state in 1850 and drew roughly 300,000 migrants from across the U.S. and abroad. Here are the most useful records and repositories:

### Key Record Sources

- **1852 California State Census** — largely name-searchable; a valuable substitute for missing federal records
- **1850 Federal Census** — partly destroyed with some county returns missing
- **Indexed county birth and marriage collections** — available for many California counties
- **Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco** — held at the **National Archives, Pacific Region (San Bruno, CA)**; covers arrivals by sea around Cape Horn or via Panama
- **San Francisco mining claim registers** and **Sacramento port arrival registers** — browse-only (not fully indexed), must be read page by page
- **Mining claims** — recorded at **county recorders' offices**

### Major Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **National Archives — Pacific Region, San Bruno** | Ship passenger manifests, federal census records |
| **Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley)** | Gold Rush manuscripts, diaries, correspondence |
| **California State Library** | Gold Rush manuscripts, state records |
| **County Recorders' Offices** | Mining claims, deeds, local vital records |

### Research Notes

- The FamilySearch catalog returned no hits for some collections — this is likely a cataloguing gap, not proof that records are absent
- Many 49ers arrived by ship, so passenger lists are especially important for tracing origins
- County-level records vary significantly in survival and accessibility
- The next logical step is building a research plan to prioritize which sources to search first based on what you know about your ancestor

Would you like to build a research plan targeting one of these record sets, or do you have a specific person in mind?

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## California Genealogy — Gold Rush Records
The California Gold Rush (1848-1855) drew hundreds of thousands of migrants. Key genealogical sources include: ship passenger manifests at San Francisco (held at the National Archives, San Bruno), overland trail diaries and journals, mining claim records at county recorders' offices, the California state census of 1852, and the Great Registers (voter registration records beginning in 1866). The California State Library and the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley hold extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records]

## California Genealogy — Pre-Statehood Records
Before American control, California was part of Spanish colonial territory and then Mexico. Mission records (1769-1834) maintained by Franciscan friars document baptisms, marriages, and burials. The 1850 federal census, the first taken in California, is essential for Gold Rush-era research but was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records]

# Locality Guide: California during the Gold Rush migration (1850-1859)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California became a state in 1850, bypassing territorial status (Wikipedia, California Gold Rush). Gold was found at Sutter's Mill in January 1848.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not returned by this survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States.
- **Population during period:** The survey returned no population figures ("none found").
- **Economy:** Gold mining drew roughly 300,000 migrants from the rest of the United States and abroad (Wikipedia).
- **Ethnic composition:** The migrant population was transient and predominantly male, from diverse origins (Wikipedia). No further breakdown was returned.
- **Religious denominations:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Key historical events:** The Gold Rush (1848 onward) drove the 1850s migration; the 1850 federal census was partly destroyed.
- **Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California; 3 are detailed here. The Catalog returned 0 hits.

## Boundary changes
- Statehood in 1850 changed California from Spanish, then Mexican, control to American jurisdiction; the survey returned no county boundary changes for the 1850s.
- Mission records (1769-1850) predate the American period and are listed as background only.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the 1852 California State Census volume (image group 006601001), which is 88% name-searchable and full-text searchable, covering 1850-1852. Next, the indexed County Births and County Marriages collections. Then the browse-only San Francisco mining claim register (1849-1855, image group 006601002) and Sacramento port arrival register (1849-1858, image group 006601003), which must be read image by image.
- Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco are held at the National Archives, San Bruno, per the [FamilySearch Wiki, California Genealogy: Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).
- Mining claims were recorded at county recorders' offices, per the same [Wiki section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records). Search the county where the claim lay.
- Overland trail diaries and journals, and Gold Rush manuscript collections, are held at the Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and the California State Library, per the same Wiki section.
- Because migrants came from other states and abroad, search the origin-state and foreign records as well. The survey did not list neighbouring-state repositories.
- The Catalog returned no hits, which is a cataloguing gap and not proof that the records do not exist. The FamilySearch Wiki home page for California returned only generic content.

FamilySearch's own digitized holdings for 1700s New York City are relatively thin compared to the historical importance of the region. home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records

question.content:
## New York City Genealogy — Colonial Records
New York City's colonial records span the Dutch (1626-1664) and British (1664-1783) periods. Key sources for the 1700s include: Dutch Reformed Church registers (the oldest continuous series, beginning 1639), Anglican (Trinity Church) and Presbyterian church records, the New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives, court records of the Mayor's Court, and land conveyances. The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society hold extensive colonial-era collections.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records]

## New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records
Colonial New York Province maintained militia rolls that list men of military age, useful for identifying residents. Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards. Wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York are indexed in the Abstracts of Wills series published by the New-York Historical Society.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records]

Here is the locality guide for Virginia during the Revolutionary War period (1775–1783):

---

**Virginia Revolutionary War Records: A Locality Guide**

Virginia's records for this period are split across several repositories, and only a portion have been digitized.

### Digitized / Searchable Sources

- **FamilySearch Military Records, 1775–1783** — A collection covering Virginia military service during the Revolution; searchable by name.
- **Augusta County Court Order Book, 1775–1795** — Partly name-indexed; useful for tracing individuals through local court proceedings, which often recorded oaths of loyalty, estate matters, and wartime transactions.
- **Virginia State Tax Lists, 1782–1799** — Full-text searchable volume; because the 1790 federal census was destroyed in 1814, the 1780s county tax lists are the standard substitute for locating families in this decade.

### Physical / Undigitized Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Continental Line service records; pension and bounty-land application files |
| **Library of Virginia** | Militia records and muster rolls |
| **Virginia State Library** | Bounty-land warrants |

### Key Gaps & Notes

- The 1790 federal census for Virginia was destroyed in the 1814 burning of Washington. County personal property and land tax lists (1782 onward) are the primary substitute for locating households.
- A catalog search returned no additional digitized items, reflecting a cataloguing gap rather than an absence of records — many Virginia Revolutionary War materials remain undigitized.

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Search the FamilySearch Virginia Military 1775–1783 collection** for your family surnames.
2. **Search NARA pension and bounty-land files** (Series M804) — these often include detailed family statements that name wives, children, and counties of residence.
3. **Check the 1782 Virginia Tax List** as a census substitute to place families geographically.
4. **Search the Augusta County court order book** if your families were in the Valley of Virginia.

If you'd like to move from this overview into a planned search for specific individuals, let me know the surnames and counties you're working with.

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War
Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony. Key military record sources include: Continental Line service records and muster rolls at the National Archives (Record Group 93), Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia in Richmond, pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA Record Group 15), and the published Virginia State Navy records.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War]

## Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands
After the Revolution, Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to its veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to their land claims. County tax lists from the 1780s are among the earliest substitutes for the missing 1790 Virginia federal census, which was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands]

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Not confirmed by this survey; the place record for Virginia, United States begins +1788, which does not describe the colony that existed during 1775-1776.

- **Religious denominations:** Not confirmed by this survey; a church-records collection is listed (1598230) without denominations.
- **Key historical events:** Virginia played a central role in the American Revolution (1775-1783), contributed more troops than any other state, and hosted the Yorktown campaign (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia).

## Boundary changes
- The survey returned no boundary-change information for Virginia; the place record for Virginia, United States carries a date range beginning +1788.
- The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Military Records page names the Virginia Military District of Ohio as the area of post-war bounty grants (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).
- Boundary changes affecting the 1775-1783 period were not confirmed by any tool result.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the FamilySearch collection 1945678 Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783, then the indexed county court volume (Augusta, image group 005301448, 61% name-indexed). The locality guide for New Orleans (Orleans Parish, Louisiana, 1800–1830) turned up the following on record survival and substitutes:

---

## What Survived — and What to Use Instead

### The 1788 and 1794 Fires
New Orleans lost most of its colonial-era records in two devastating French Quarter fires. This means very few records from before 1800 survive in original form.

### Records That Do Survive for the Early 1800s

| Record Type | Where Held | Coverage |
|---|---|---|
| **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) | Cathedral / microfilm | From 1731, with gaps caused by the fires |
| **Notarial acts** | New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | From 1734; reportedly over 30 million pages |
| **Cabildo / Spanish colonial government records** | Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Pre-1803 territorial period |
| **Territorial and early state records** | Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Post-1803 |

### The Notarial Archive — The Most Important Substitute
Notarial acts recorded sales, successions, contracts, manumissions, and many life events that civil registers would otherwise capture. A surviving microfilm volume covers **1803–1820**, but it is not name-indexed — you must browse image by image. The guide found only this one volume available online.

### Floods, Hurricanes, and Yellow Fever
These events also damaged archives over the years, but no source the guide consulted names a specific record set that was destroyed by them. The guide's advice: **search for surviving copies or microfilm before assuming a record is lost.**

### A Gap to Note
The FamilySearch catalog returned no entries for New Orleans — this appears to be a cataloguing gap rather than proof the records don't exist. The Louisiana State Archives and the Notarial Archives Research Center are the right repositories to contact or visit directly.

---

The guide has been saved as **loc_001** in your project. A logical next step would be to build a research plan starting with the cathedral sacramental registers and the notarial volume.

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters
New Orleans suffered catastrophic fires in 1788 and 1794 that destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records. Despite these losses, significant genealogical sources survive for the early 1800s: sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, though with gaps), notarial records, and the records of the Cabildo (Spanish colonial governing body). The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]

## Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records
Louisiana's parish-based civil law system (unlike the county-based common law of other US states) means that many legal records are unique to Louisiana: successions (probate), tutorships (guardianship), and interdictions. The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System]

agent_returns.text:
Saved locality guide loc_001 for New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana, covering 1800 to 1830, which I took as the early 1800s.

---

The guide says New Orleans lost most of its colonial-era records in fires in 1788 and 1794, which destroyed most of the French Quarter. Records that survive for the early 1800s are the St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages and burials from 1731, with gaps), the notarial acts, and the Cabildo records of the Spanish colonial government. The notarial archive is the most important: the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center reportedly holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734. The guide found only a single notarial volume online, covering 1803 to 1820 on surviving microfilm copies. It is not searchable by name, so it has to be browsed image by image. Floods, hurricanes and yellow fever epidemics also damaged archives, but no source the guide consulted names a specific record set lost to them, so you should look for surviving copies before assuming a loss. The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records. The FamilySearch catalog returned no entries for New Orleans, which is a gap in cataloguing rather than proof that the records do not exist.

Next, the parentage question for Jean Baptiste Fortier still needs a search plan, which research-plan can build from this guide, starting with the cathedral registers and the notarial volume.

Here is what the locality-guide found:

---

**Boston Port of Entry Records, 1840s — Locality Guide**

**Saved as:** loc_001

---

### Key Record Type: Customs Passenger Lists
The primary source for 1840s Boston arrivals is the **Customs Passenger Lists for the Port of Boston (1820–1891)**, which FamilySearch has indexed. However, the volume covering **1840–1850 is only ~3% name-indexed**, meaning most of it must be searched via:
- **Full-text search** (FamilySearch's AI-transcribed documents), or
- **Image browsing** page by page

Information typically recorded in 1840s lists is minimal: name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — no hometown or next of kin.

---

### Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston** (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger list manuscripts |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers from the 1840s onward — especially valuable for Irish immigrants |

---

### Research Notes
- A FamilySearch Catalog search returned no results for Boston, which appears to be a cataloguing gap rather than an absence of records.
- The next step would be to use the **research-plan** or **search-records** agent to execute searches against the indexed and full-text portions of the passenger lists.
- If the ancestor was Irish Catholic, **parish registers** in Boston (baptisms, marriages, burials) may supplement the sparse arrival data.

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

## Massachusetts Immigration — Port of Boston
Boston was one of the five major US ports of entry in the 1840s, receiving tens of thousands of Irish Famine immigrants. Customs passenger lists (1820-1891) for the Port of Boston are in National Archives Record Group 36 and have been indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Unlike later Ellis Island-era manifests, 1840s lists typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin. The National Archives at Boston (Waltham) holds the originals.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston]

## Massachusetts Church Records — Boston Area Churches
Church records are essential for tracing Boston immigrants who arrived before civil vital registration became comprehensive. Catholic parish registers (especially those of the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's) document baptisms, marriages, and burials of Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward. The Archdiocese of Boston archives holds these records.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston]

Here is what the locality-guide found and recorded in your project:

---

**Oklahoma / Indian Territory — Mid-1800s Tribal Records Locality Guide**

Oklahoma didn't become a state until 1907, so for the mid-1800s the relevant jurisdiction is **Indian Territory**. The guide was surveyed for the period 1840–1870.

---

### Collections Confirmed by the Survey

The following were found and logged in your project (loc_001):

1. **Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959** — The key tribal-roll series, with coverage that overlaps your mid-century window. Search within it by nation name for 1851–1870 entries.

2. **Oklahoma Land Records, 1834–1907** — Land transactions and allotment records covering Indian Territory.

3. **Oklahoma Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965** — Mission congregations served many tribal communities; these can fill gaps when civil records don't exist.

4. **Tribal Enrollment Cards (name-searchable volume)** — A fully indexed volume of enrollment cards useful for locating specific individuals.

---

### Critical Repository Not in the FamilySearch Catalog

**National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)** holds the federal treaty and Indian records. These include:

- **Record Group 75** — Bureau of Indian Affairs records, including agency correspondence, annuity rolls, and census rolls for the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Muscogee, and Seminole)
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** — The definitive enrollment record for the Five Tribes; though compiled after your period, it names relatives and traces lineage back into the mid-1800s
- **Wallace Roll, Drennen Roll, Chapman Roll, and other pre-Dawes tribal rolls** — Earlier rolls (1850s–1880s) for specific nations

NARA's Southwest Region in Fort Worth, Texas is the primary repository for Indian Territory federal records.

---

### Additional Repositories to Consult

- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — Holds extensive tribal records, including Cherokee Nation records, Choctaw records, and Indian Territory court files
- **Cherokee Nation Archives (Tahlequah, OK)** — Original Cherokee citizenship and census records
- **Five Civilized Tribes Museum** — Supplementary research resources
- **University of Oklahoma Western History Collections** — Manuscript collections related to tribal history

---

### Next Steps

1. Search the **Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959** collection on FamilySearch by nation name
2. Check **NARA Record Group 75** for the specific tribe(s) you are researching
3. Work backward from the **Dawes Rolls** to identify mid-century ancestors
4. Search tribal-specific archives (Cherokee, Choctaw, etc.) if you know which nation the family belonged to

The guide is now saved to your project as **loc_001** for future reference.

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

Here's the locality guide for Quaker research in late-1700s Pennsylvania:

---

For Quaker families in late-1700s Pennsylvania, the best trail runs through the **meeting records themselves**. Monthly meetings recorded:

- **Births, marriages, and deaths**
- **Certificates of removal** (when a family moved between meetings)
- **Disownments**

These records often stood in for civil registration, since Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration until 1906.

## Key Finding Aids & Repositories

- **William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** — a published six-volume set of Quaker genealogy abstracts; an essential starting point.
- **Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College** — holds the largest collection of American Quaker records.
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes (1750–1800)** — available as a browse-only image volume, but it has no name index and must be read page by page.

## Geography

The densest Quaker populations were in **Chester, Bucks, and Philadelphia counties**, so those are the highest-priority meetings to search.

## Strategy

The survey found no catalogued meeting registers in the FamilySearch catalog — that is a gap in the catalog, not proof the records don't exist. The recommended approach is to:

1. Search meeting records **meeting by meeting**, starting with Chester, Bucks, and Philadelphia.
2. Identify the family's specific meeting.
3. Follow **removal certificates** to trace the family as they moved between meetings.

question.content:
## Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker (Friends) Records
Quaker (Society of Friends) meeting records are among the most detailed religious records in Pennsylvania. Monthly meetings recorded births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (transfers between meetings), and disciplinary proceedings (disownments). Marriage certificates were signed by all attendees. Quaker records often substitute for civil registration, which Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide until 1906. The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College holds the largest collection of American Quaker records.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records]

## Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts
William Wade Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy (6 volumes) abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states. FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers. Chester County, Bucks County, and Philadelphia had particularly dense Quaker populations in the colonial and early national periods.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts]

---

## Pittsburgh, PA — Late 1800s Steel Industry: Records & Repositories

### Federal Census (1870–1900)
The most broadly useful source — occupation fields identify steel workers, laborers, and mill employees. Household members, ages, birthplaces, and neighbors are all captured.

### City Directories
Held at the **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh**, these annual directories list residents by name, occupation, and address — invaluable for tracking mill workers year by year between censuses.

### Company Employment Records
Surviving records from the steel mills are fragmentary. The best repositories to contact are:
- **Heinz History Center** (Senator John Heinz History Center)
- **Rivers of Steel** archives — focused specifically on the steel industry heritage

### Church / Parish Records
Pittsburgh's steel workforce was heavily immigrant (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian). **Catholic parish registers** often provide the richest family details — baptisms, marriages, burials — though verifying which parish served a specific family will require additional research.

### Civil Vital Records (State)
Pennsylvania death and marriage records for this era are **indexed and searchable online**.

### Probate & Naturalization Records
These Allegheny County records have been digitized but are **unindexed** — they must be browsed image-by-image (available on FamilySearch).

---

**Suggested next step:** Use `research-plan` on this guide to build specific searches for the families you're tracing.

question.content:
## Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial and Occupational Records
Pittsburgh's steel industry employed hundreds of thousands of workers in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Genealogical sources for industrial workers include: company employment records (fragmentary — some survive at the Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel archives), union membership lists, city directories that list occupations, federal census schedules (1870-1900 list occupation), and state factory inspector reports. The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh has a strong local history collection including city directories from the 1810s.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records]

## Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records
The massive immigration to Pittsburgh's steel mills in the late 1800s is documented in naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia. Church records are essential — Catholic parishes served specific ethnic communities (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian), and their registers are often the best source for family data.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records]

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pittsburgh is recorded from 1758 and Allegheny County from 1788 in the place standard (place_search); the survey did not return a formation narrative.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by this survey for Allegheny County; Pittsburgh is the city in the standard place.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States.
- **Population during period:** The survey returned no population figures ("none found").
- **Economy:** The FamilySearch Wiki says Pittsburgh's steel industry employed hundreds of thousands of workers in the late 1800s and early 1900s, with fragmentary company employment records.
- **Ethnic composition:** Polish, Slovak, Croatian and Italian communities, served by Catholic parishes, per the FamilySearch Wiki Allegheny County immigration section.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes serving ethnic communities are named; the survey did not return a fuller list.
- **Key historical events:** The survey returned no events affecting records for 1880-1900.
- **Coverage of this survey:** The volume summary counts 3 volumes for Pittsburgh and 3 listed; all 3 listed are the probate, death and naturalization image groups. The Catalog returned 0 hits.

args.guideSection:
## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the 1880-1900 federal census for occupation, the city directories at the Carnegie Library, and the Pennsylvania death and marriage collections (2255317 and 1921317, indexed). Then check the naturalization image group (008120443, 15% name-indexed) and the probate image group (008120441), which are browse-only. Company employment records are last, because they are fragmentary.
- **Industrial sources:** The FamilySearch Wiki names company employment records, union membership lists, city directories listing occupations, federal census schedules for 1870-1900, and state factory inspector reports for Allegheny County, at [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy, Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records). Company records are fragmentary and may survive at the Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel archives.
- **Immigrant families:** Catholic parish registers served Polish, Slovak, Croatian and Italian communities, and the wiki calls them often the best family source, per the [Immigration Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records). The survey did not confirm which parish served a given family.
- **Naturalizations:** The wiki places them at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia, per the same immigration section.
- **Alternative sources:** Where a steel-mill record is missing, use city directories for occupation and the census for household details, and the neighbouring-county records as a cross-border check.
- **Finding aids:** The [Genealogy Research Guide](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide) covers the general record types; the survey did not return further Pittsburgh-specific finding aids.

loc_001 written for Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1880-1900).

---

I built a locality guide for Pittsburgh covering 1880 to 1900, which I took as your "late 1800s." Tell me if you meant a narrower span. The most useful records for tracing steel workers are the federal census, which lists occupations for 1870 to 1900, and the city directories at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh. ## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the 1880-1900 federal census for occupation, the city directories at the Carnegie Library, and the Pennsylvania death and marriage collections (2255317 and 1921317, indexed). Then check the naturalization image group (008120443, 15% name-indexed) and the probate image group (008120441), which are browse-only. Company employment records are last, because they are fragmentary.

**Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic: Records & Repositories**

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793
The 1793 yellow fever epidemic killed approximately 5,000 of Philadelphia's 50,000 residents. Key genealogical sources include: burial records from Christ Church, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes'), and other churches; the published account by Mathew Carey listing names of the dead; minutes and reports of the Committee appointed by the citizens; and the records of Bush Hill hospital. The Historical Society of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia City Archives hold manuscript sources.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793]

## Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records
Philadelphia's church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906. The city's diverse religious communities each maintained registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials. Many colonial and early national church registers have been transcribed and published. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records]

output.text_response:
Here is what the locality-guide agent found for tracing families affected by the 1871 Chicago Fire:

---

**The Great Chicago Fire and Record Loss**

The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and most of the city's earliest records — deeds, probate files, and many church registers. This is one of the most significant record losses in American genealogical research.

**What Survived and Where to Find It**

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **National Archives / FamilySearch** | The **1870 federal census** for Chicago survived because originals were held in Washington, D.C. — a critical resource for pre-fire households. |
| **Cook County Circuit Court / IRAD** | Reconstructed pre-fire court records and post-fire property re-recordings. Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University holds post-1871 county records. |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Insurance records and fire-related documentation. |
| **Newberry Library** | City directories from the 1840s onward — invaluable for locating families before and after the fire. |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago Archives** | Catholic parish registers; post-fire Catholic church records are largely intact. |

**Key Research Strategies for Fire Survivors**

1. **1870 federal census** — Establishes pre-fire household composition.
2. **1880 federal census** — Shows who was still in Chicago and family reconstitution.
3. **Post-fire city directories (1872+)** — Track family re-establishment and new addresses.
4. **Probate records** — Post-1871 Cook County probate at IRAD may show heirs if a family head died in or around the fire.
5. **Insurance claims** — Chicago History Museum holds fire-related insurance records.
6. **Newspaper accounts** — Relief lists and survivor notices were published in the *Chicago Tribune* and other papers; check newspaper archives (Newspapers.com, Chronicling America).
7. **Church records** — Catholic archives survived relatively well; Protestant denominations vary — contact individual denominational archives.

**Important Caveat**

The guide could not confirm surviving probate series, Chicago-specific military or tax records for 1871, or records for all Protestant denominations. Additional verification through the repositories above is recommended before concluding a record type is lost.

This locality guide has been saved to the project as **loc_001** for future reference.

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire
The Great Chicago Fire of October 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and most of the city's early records, including deeds, probate files, and many church registers. Genealogists must use substitute sources: reconstructed deeds filed under the Burnt Record Act (1872), church registers from parishes that survived or were re-established, insurance company records (especially the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum), and federal census schedules (1850, 1860, 1870 — the 1870 for Chicago survived because originals were in Washington). City directories from the 1840s onward also survived and are held at the Newberry Library.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire]

## Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records (1699–1762)
French colonial Louisiana (1699–1762) produced several categories of genealogical records. Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary source for family data — the Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana, and the Code Noir required baptism of all enslaved persons. The St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from 1720. The Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) records include land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories. These records are held at the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building (New Orleans) and have been partially digitized. The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds administrative correspondence and census rolls for the colony.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records]

## Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants
Colonial-era land grants in Louisiana followed French and Spanish legal traditions, not English common law. French concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and in records at the Louisiana State Land Office. Notarial archives in New Orleans (the oldest continuous notarial office in North America) hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center provides public access.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants]

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records (1699–1762)
French colonial Louisiana (1699–1762) produced several categories of genealogical records. Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary source for family data — the Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana, and the Code Noir required baptism of all enslaved persons. The St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from 1720. The Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) records include land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories. These records are held at the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building (New Orleans) and have been partially digitized. The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds administrative correspondence and census rolls for the colony.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records]

## Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants
Colonial-era land grants in Louisiana followed French and Spanish legal traditions, not English common law. French concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and in records at the Louisiana State Land Office. Notarial archives in New Orleans (the oldest continuous notarial office in North America) hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center provides public access.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants]

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records (1699–1762)
French colonial Louisiana (1699–1762) produced several categories of genealogical records. Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary source for family data — the Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana, and the Code Noir required baptism of all enslaved persons. The St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from 1720. The Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) records include land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories. These records are held at the Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building (New Orleans) and have been partially digitized. The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France holds administrative correspondence and census rolls for the colony.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records]

## Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants
Colonial-era land grants in Louisiana followed French and Spanish legal traditions, not English common law. French concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and in records at the Louisiana State Land Office. Notarial archives in New Orleans (the oldest continuous notarial office in North America) hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center provides public access.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants]

Here is what the locality-guide found for Pennsylvania coal mining towns in the late 1800s:

---

**Locality Survey: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (c. 1870–1900)**

The survey focused on **Schuylkill County** (a core anthracite coal county) but also covers neighboring **Luzerne and Lackawanna Counties**.

### Key Record Types and Repositories

**Mine/Employment Records**
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards** — well-indexed and name-searchable; one of the best sources for identifying miners by name.
- **Coal-company payroll ledgers and mine accident reports** (Luzerne/Lackawanna) — exist but are only browsable image-by-image with no name index.
- **Pennsylvania State Mine Inspector Reports (from 1870)** — name men killed in accidents; useful for locating family members.

**Census**
- U.S. Federal Censuses (1870–1900) list occupation as "miner," making it possible to identify coal-mining households.

**Vital Records**
- **Pennsylvania statewide death certificates** are only indexed from **1906 onward**. For deaths before that date, you must rely on church records, probate, and newspaper death notices.

**Church Records**
- **Ethnic parish registers** (Catholic, Orthodox, etc.) serving the immigrant mining communities are often the most detailed family source, with baptisms, marriages, and burials. The specific parishes serving individual towns would need to be confirmed.

**Repositories to Check**
- **Pennsylvania State Archives** — holds original payrolls, accident reports, and state agency records.
- **Local historical societies** in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna Counties — hold fragmentary company and community records.

---

**Suggested Next Step:** The `research-plan` agent can turn this guide into a sequenced search plan — starting with the employment cards and the 1870–1900 censuses — if you have a specific ancestor in mind.

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining Records
Pennsylvania's coal mining regions generated distinctive genealogical records. Company employment records (payrolls, accident reports) survive fragmentarily at the Pennsylvania State Archives and at local historical societies in Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Lackawanna counties. The state Mine Inspector reports (published annually from 1870) list fatal accidents with names, ages, nationalities, and cause of death. Church records are essential — ethnic parishes (Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic) served specific mining communities and their registers often contain the most detailed family data. Federal census schedules (1870–1900) list occupation as 'miner' and can identify mining families.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining]

## Research tips
- **Search order:** start with the Mine Worker Employment Cards (image group 002240015, 1870-1900, 95% name-searchable) because they are indexed and name miners directly. Next, the 1870-1900 federal census for occupation "miner" (Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining). Then the browse-only Luzerne accident reports and Lackawanna payroll ledgers, read image by image.
- Church registers are essential for the period because the wiki says ethnic parishes often hold the most detailed family data (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining). The parish for a given town is not confirmed by this survey.
- Search the state Mine Inspector reports, published from 1870, for fatal accidents with names, ages and nationalities (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining).
- Search across the border into Luzerne and Lackawanna counties, because mining families moved between coal-field counties; the survey did not list adjoining counties.
- Substitutes when series are missing: newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/), Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) and the 1906 death certificate index for later deaths. The wiki says negative online results do not prove absence; records may be undigitized, unindexed or held only in a physical repository (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide).

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** the place_search date range for Schuylkill County begins 1811; the parent jurisdiction and formation details were not confirmed by this survey.
- **County seat / administrative center:** not confirmed by this survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States.
- **Population during period:** the survey returned no population figures.
- **Economy:** anthracite coal mining; company payrolls and mine accident reports are the coal-specific records (Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining).
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic and Lithuanian Catholic parishes served mining communities per the wiki; the survey did not give local percentages.
- **Religious denominations:** as listed in the wiki excerpt above.
- **Key historical events:** not confirmed by this survey.
- **Coverage of this survey:** the volume list shows 3 of 23 matching Schuylkill volumes; the catalog returned 0 hits for Schuylkill and Pennsylvania.

## Boundary changes
- The survey did not return any boundary changes for Schuylkill County during 1870-1900.
- Records before formation or any predecessor jurisdiction were not confirmed by this survey.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** start with the Mine Worker Employment Cards (image group 002240015, 1870-1900, 95% name-searchable) because they are indexed and name miners directly. Next, the 1870-1900 federal census for occupation "miner" (Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining). Then the browse-only Luzerne accident reports and Lackawanna payroll ledgers, read image by image.
- Church registers are essential for the period because the wiki says ethnic parishes often hold the most detailed family data (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining). The parish for a given town is not confirmed by this survey.
- Search the state Mine Inspector reports, published from 1870, for fatal accidents with names, ages and nationalities (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining).
- Search across the border into Luzerne and Lackawanna counties, because mining families moved between coal-field counties; the survey did not list adjoining counties.

The wiki says negative online results do not prove absence; records may be undigitized, unindexed or held only in a physical repository (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide).

The locality guide has been saved to your project as **loc_001**. Here is a summary of what it found for **Massachusetts, 1600–1650 (Colonial Puritan Period)**:

---

### Key Record Types and Repositories

**Town Vital Records**
- Massachusetts required towns to record births, marriages, and deaths from **1639** onward. These are among the earliest and most useful sources for this period.

**Congregational Church Registers**
- Puritan congregations kept their own membership, baptism, and burial records. Availability varies by parish; some Suffolk County volumes are searchable full-text, while others must be browsed image by image.

**Probate & Deed Records**
- County courts and registries begin in the **1630s**. Middlesex, Suffolk, and Essex County probate records are the main starting points.

**Colony Court Records**
- Held at the **Massachusetts Archives (Boston)** — includes colonial court records from the 1630s.

**Great Migration Series**
- The **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS, Boston)** holds and publishes the *Great Migration* series, which documents individual settlers who arrived **1620–1643**. This is essential for the Puritan settlement era.

**Plymouth Colony Records**
- Kept separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. If your families were in Plymouth, search those records independently.

---

### Gaps for This Period
- **No census records** (US federal census began 1790; colonial-era enumerations are rare)
- **No confirmed military, tax, or newspaper records** found for 1600–1650
- FamilySearch Catalog search returned no hits for this period specifically

---

### Suggested Next Step
Turn this record survey into a **research plan** targeting your specific families — the town vital records and Great Migration series would be the logical first searches.

Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records
Massachusetts has among the earliest and most complete vital records in North America. The colony mandated town recording of births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639. Published compilations include the multi-volume 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series (known as the Tanner–Corbin series), which abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. The Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds the original colony records, governor's correspondence, and court records from the 1620s onward. The New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) in Boston has the largest genealogical research library in New England, including manuscript collections, published genealogies, and the 'Great Migration' study series documenting every known settler who arrived 1620–1643.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records]

## Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational Church Records
Congregational church records are central to early Massachusetts genealogy. As the established church of the colony, Congregational meetings kept registers of members, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary actions (excommunications, admonishments). Many early church records have been published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and in local historical society publications. Land records (deeds) were recorded at the county level from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds. Probate records begin in the 1630s at county probate courts. Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are published and indexed separately.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational]

Here is the locality guide for **Oklahoma during the Land Run of 1889** (saved as loc_001 in your project):

---

The Land Run of 1889 opened part of what is now Oklahoma to settlement, and the land was organized as **Oklahoma Territory in 1890** before statehood in 1907. The most useful records and repositories for families of this era include:

### Key Record Types & Repositories

**Federal Homestead Files**
- The Land Run itself generated homestead/claim files held at the **National Archives, Washington, D.C.**
- The **Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office Records** site offers a free searchable index of federal land patents.

**Territorial Court Records (1890–1907)**
- Civil, criminal, probate, and naturalization records are held at the:
  - **National Archives at Fort Worth**
  - **Oklahoma State Archives** (Oklahoma City)

**1890 Territorial Special Census**
- The **Oklahoma Historical Society** holds this special enumeration taken shortly after the Land Run opened the territory.

**Vital Records**
- Pre-statehood vital records are sparse. Some counties kept incomplete birth and death registers from 1891 at the **county courthouse**; marriages before 1890 are limited.
- Land, court, and probate records will carry more weight than vital records for this period.

---

**Practical tip:** Because vital records are thin before 1908, the homestead files and territorial court records (especially probate) are your best anchors for tracing families who arrived in the 1889 Land Run.

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).
