question.content:
## Oklahoma Land Records — Land Run and Homestead Records
The Land Run of 1889 and subsequent openings generated extensive federal land records. Homestead applications, final certificates, and land patents are held at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. (Record Group 49, General Land Office) and have been partially indexed on FamilySearch and the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office Records website (glorecords.blm.gov). Each homestead file typically includes the original application, proof of settlement (with witnesses), and the final patent. Rejected applications also survive and can contain family details. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds territorial and early state records, including the Oklahoma Territory census (1890 special census, one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation).
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run]

## Oklahoma Territorial Records — Territorial Courts and Early Settlement
Territorial court records for Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907) are at the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives. These include district court civil and criminal cases, probate, and naturalization records. Many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states — tracing their origins often requires searching departure-state records. The first territorial census (1890) and county-level tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers. Church records begin sporadically in 1889 as denominations established congregations in the new towns.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts]

## Online Oklahoma Birth, Marriage and Death Records

### Births

* [Oklahoma State Vital Records Index](https://ok2explore.health.ok.gov/App/BirthSearch) at OK2Explore
* [Early Oklahoma Birth Records](http://sites.rootsweb.com/~okgs/early_ok_birth_records.htm) at Oklahoma Genealogical Society

### Marriages

* **1600s-1900s** [US Marriages - Oklahoma, 1600's to 1900's](https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-records/united-states-marriages?state=oklahoma) at Findmypast — index ($)
* **1870-1930** [Oklahoma Marriages, 1870-1930](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1681007) at FamilySearch — [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Marriages_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "Oklahoma Marriages - FamilySearch Historical Records"); *Also at: [Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/60105)($), [MyHeritage](http://www.myheritage.com/research/collection-30202/oklahoma-marriages-1870-1930?s=218489221)($)*
* **1889-1951** [Oklahoma County, Oklahoma Marriage Index, 1889-1951](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/9233) at Ancestry — index ($)
* **1890-1995** [Oklahoma County Marriages, 1890-1995](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1709399) at FamilySearch — [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_County_Marriages_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "Oklahoma County Marriages - FamilySearch Historical Records"); index & images; *Also at: [Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/61379)($)*
* [Oklahoma Marriage Records](https://www.okhistory.org/research/marrresults) at Oklahoma Historical Society

#### Indigenous Peoples - Marriages

* [Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Marriage, Citizenship and Census Records, 1841-1927](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/9026) ($)

### Deaths

* **1864-1941** [Oklahoma Deaths and Burials, 1864-1941](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3518733) at FamilySearch — [How to Use this Collection](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma,_Death_Records_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records "Oklahoma, Death Records - FamilySearch Historical Records"); index
* [Oklahoma State Vital Records Index](https://ok2explore.health.ok.gov/App/DeathSearch) at OK2Explore

## Birth and Death Records

Some counties kept birth and death records as early as 1891, although most did not start until after statehood in 1907. The early records, which are quite incomplete, are at county courthouses. Contact details for county courts can be found on individual [county pages](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma,_United_States_Genealogy "Oklahoma, United States Genealogy"). The FamilySearch Library has copied some of the vital records of the Superintendent of Public Health in a few counties.

The statewide registration of births and deaths began in [Oklahoma](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma,_United_States_Genealogy "Oklahoma, United States Genealogy") in 1908 and was generally complied with by 1930. You can write to:

Vital Records Service  
Oklahoma State Department of Health  
1000 Northeast 10th Street, Room 111  
Oklahoma City, OK 73117  
Telephone: 405-271-4040  
[Website](https://oklahoma.gov/health/birth-and-death-certificates.html)

The current fees for obtaining copies of the state's records are listed on the Internet site above. Copies of birth records are restricted to the individual, their next of kin, or a legal representative. See the above Internet site for requirements for requesting records. Death records are not restricted.

### Accessibility to Oklahoma Birth and Death Records

Oklahoma vital records are protected by state law, 63 O.S. Sec. 1-323 (Effective Nov 1, 2016). Birth records that are at 125 years old and records of death at least 50 years old are considered open records. However, as stated on the [Oklahoma State Department of Health](https://oklahoma.gov/health/birth-and-death-certificates/genealogists.html): “…a genealogist will need written permission from the subject (if alive) or a family member if the subject is deceased. Proof of relationship between the family member and the deceased will be required.”

A list of who can request a vital record is contained on the [Oklahoma State Department of Health’s website](https://oklahoma.gov/health/birth-and-death-certificates/genealogists.html) and is also in the state law. The state does provide a free searchable index of births and deaths that occurred in the state of Oklahoma and is available at: [Ok2Explore](https://ok2explore.health.ok.gov/). If you are eligible to receive a record and want a certified copy of the record you can apply online through a [partner website](https://www.vitalchek.com/vital-records/oklahoma/oklahoma-vital-records?click_id=646266980319952898&ppc=0) or by phone (or mail) to the Vital Records Service. You will have to pick up the record in Oklahoma City and provide proof of eligibility to receive the record.

### Delayed Birth Records

Delayed registrations of births (for persons born before registration began in 1908) are available from the Vital Records Service mentioned above.

## Marriage Records

Before 1890, no marriages were recorded by the county or state. 1830's to 1889 very few records exist, some recorded in district courts.

Oklahoma became a state in 1907. Prior to statehood it was Indian Territory from the 1830's to 1890. In 1890 Oklahoma was divided into two Territories (Twin Territories) Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory.

In 1890 three Judicial Districts were established where marriages could be performed and recorded:

* First District: at Muskogee included Cherokee and Creek Nations
* Second District: at South McAlester included Choctaw Nation

---

The Land Run of 1889 opened part of what is now Oklahoma to settlement, and the land was organized as Oklahoma Territory in 1890 before statehood in 1907. The most useful records for these families are the federal homestead files from the Land Run openings, held at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. Some of those files are indexed online, and the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office records site offers a free index. Territorial court records (civil and criminal cases, probate, naturalization) are at the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives, and the Oklahoma Historical Society holds the 1890 territorial special census. Vital records are thin before 1908: some counties kept incomplete birth and death records from 1891 at the courthouse, and marriages before 1890 are sparse, so the court and land files will carry more weight.

Next, I can help you check your own project's objective, which concerns Patrick Flynn's parents in Pennsylvania, to see whether these Oklahoma records bear on it or whether a separate Pennsylvania guide is needed.

# Locality Guide: Land Run of 1889 settlement area and Oklahoma Territory (1889-1907)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma became a state in 1907; before 1890 the area was Indian Territory, and in 1890 it was divided into Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory (Oklahoma_Vital_Records).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Oklahoma Territory (1890-1907), following the 1889 Land Run openings.
- **Population during period:** The survey returned no population figures; the 1890 territorial special census is listed under census.
- **Economy:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** Not confirmed by this survey; many settlers came from Kansas, Texas and Missouri (Oklahoma_Territorial_Records).
- **Religious denominations:** Not confirmed by this survey; church records begin sporadically in 1889 (Oklahoma_Territorial_Records).
- **Key historical events:** The 1889 Land Run and later openings generated federal homestead files (Oklahoma_Land_Records).
- **Coverage of this survey:** Volumes: 2 digitized volumes matched at the state level and both are listed. Catalog returned 0 hits at the state and national levels.

## Boundary changes
- 1889: Land Run openings of Unassigned Lands (Oklahoma_Land_Records).
- 1890: Oklahoma divided into Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory; three judicial districts established for marriages (Oklahoma_Vital_Records).
- 1907: Statehood; the state vital registration begins in 1908 (Oklahoma_Vital_Records).
- The survey did not confirm county boundary changes for this period.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the federal homestead files, since the Land Run generated them: the digitized land-entry case files (image group 005221388, 1889-1907) are 74% name-searchable, and the BLM General Land Office index is at glorecords.blm.gov (Oklahoma_Land_Records). Next, search the court and county series: territorial district court records at the National Archives at Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives, and the 1890s county tax rolls (Oklahoma_Territorial_Records). Then browse the offline ones: the Dawes enrollment jackets (image group 005221389) are 0% name-searchable and must be read image by image.
- Vital records before 1908 are thin: some counties kept incomplete birth and death records from 1891 at the courthouse, and marriages before 1890 are sparse (Oklahoma_Vital_Records). Use the OK2Explore statewide index for later deaths.
- Many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas and Missouri; search the departure states for their origins (Oklahoma_Territorial_Records).
- The 1890 territorial special census is one of the few surviving 1890 census records nationally (Oklahoma_Land_Records).

---

## Alabama Region, circa 1800 — Locality Research Guide

**Jurisdictional Context**

Alabama did not exist as a state in 1800. The land that is now Alabama was part of **Mississippi Territory** (1798–1817), then **Alabama Territory** (1817–1819), before achieving statehood in 1819. Any research for the Alabama region in this period must be framed under those territorial designations.

---

### Record Types Available

**Territorial Censuses**
Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** — these are the primary substitutes for the missing 1800 federal census in this area. The originals are held by the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery.

**Land Records**
Land transactions are among the best-surviving record sets for this period. Territorial land records are available through FamilySearch collections categorized under Mississippi, though it is not confirmed which of those collections specifically cover the Alabama counties.

**County Court Records**
County courts were active even during the territorial period. FamilySearch has collections of Mississippi territorial and county court records, though again the coverage of present-day Alabama counties within those collections is not fully confirmed.

**Church Records**
Some early church records exist, though survival is sparse for this era and region.

**Colonial Records (Mobile Area)**
The Mobile area has a distinct colonial heritage — French, British, and then Spanish rule preceded American territorial status. Colonial-era records are held in archives in **France, Spain, and Mobile itself**, making them harder to access but potentially valuable for families in that corridor.

---

### Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery) | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810), county records |
| FamilySearch (under "Mississippi") | Land, court, census substitute, and church record collections |
| Archives in France & Spain | French and Spanish colonial records for the Mobile area |
| Mobile local archives | British and Spanish colonial records |

---

### On Digitized, Browsable Volumes

The survey found **no digitized browsable volumes** in FamilySearch's catalog specifically identified for this territory and period — and no catalog entries at all turned up. That is a **gap in the survey**, not proof that such volumes don't exist. The recommended next steps for browsable images are:

1. Search the **FamilySearch Catalog** directly under "Mississippi Territory" and under individual county names (e.g., Madison County, Washington County) for image groups.
2. Contact or browse the **Alabama Department of Archives and History** digital collections at [adah.alabama.gov](https://adah.alabama.gov) — they have been digitizing territorial-era materials.

---

### Suggested Next Steps

- Plan searches starting with the **1805 and 1810 territorial censuses** (the two most useful census substitutes for this window).
- Search FamilySearch land record collections filed under "Mississippi" for the Alabama counties that were organized during the territorial period.
- If ancestry traces to the Mobile corridor, pursue the Spanish colonial records separately — those predate American territorial administration entirely.

# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records
Alabama was part of the Mississippi Territory from 1798 to 1817, then became the Alabama Territory until statehood in 1819. Territorial records include land grants, tax lists, militia rolls, and court records. The earliest land records are Spanish and British colonial grants in the Mobile area. The Mississippi Territory census of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These territorial censuses are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records]

## Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records
Before American control, the Mobile area was administered by France (1702-1763), Britain (1763-1780), and Spain (1780-1813). French colonial records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence and in microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish records of the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records]

# Locality Guide: Mississippi Territory, United States (1795-1805)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Mississippi Territory was formed in 1798 (place record date range +1798/1817). The present-day Alabama region was part of it.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (territorial government).
- **Population during period:** The survey found no population figures for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** Not confirmed by this survey beyond the wiki's note that the Mobile area was under French, British and then Spanish control.
- **Religious denominations:** Not confirmed by this survey.
- **Key historical events:** Colonial control of the Mobile area passed from France (1702-1763) to Britain (1763-1780) to Spain (1780-1813), per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Coverage of this survey:** Volumes: 0 digitized volumes matched for Mississippi Territory, and the catalog returned 0 hits. This is a survey gap, not proof that browsable volumes do not exist.

## Boundary changes
- Alabama was not a state in 1800. From 1798 to 1817 the present-day Alabama region was part of Mississippi Territory; it then became Alabama Territory until statehood in 1819 (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records). The request's "Alabama before statehood" therefore maps to Mississippi Territory records for this period.
- Before American control, the Mobile area was administered by France, then Britain, then Spain (1780-1813) (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- The survey did not confirm any county boundary changes within the Alabama region for 1795-1805.

## Research tips
- **Search order:** Start with the Mississippi Territory census enumerations of 1801, 1805, 1808 and 1810, held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records). Then check the FamilySearch collections 1927171 (Compiled Census and Census Substitutes), 1919694 (Territorial and State Land Records) and 1855293 (County Court Records); each is labelled Mississippi, so confirm Alabama-county coverage first. Then check church collection 2034891 and the Mobile-area colonial sources.
- **Digitized, browsable volumes:** The survey found none for Mississippi Territory (0 volumes, 0 catalog hits). Search the FamilySearch Catalog by Mississippi Territory and the Alabama counties directly, and ask ADAH whether the territorial censuses are digitized.
- **Colonial Mobile:** Records from the French, British and Spanish periods may be in French or Spanish. The wiki names the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence), the Mobile Municipal Archives (microfilm of French records) and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Alternative sources:** The survey did not confirm probate, tax, military or newspaper holdings for this period. Search for the Alabama Department of Archives and History's territorial holdings directly.
- **Finding aids:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy) is the main guide the survey returned; the general wiki home pages returned only generic content.

Here is the locality-guide agent's report:

---

**Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide (1860–1899)**

**Survey saved as `loc_001`** in your project at `/private/tmp/eval-ut_locality_guide_022-0-0-r278_cm4`.

---

### Counties Covered
The five core anthracite coal counties are:
- **Schuylkill**
- **Luzerne**
- **Lackawanna** (formed from Luzerne in 1878)
- **Northumberland**
- **Carbon**

---

### Key Finding: Coal-Region Specialized Index
The FamilySearch Wiki page on coal-region records names the **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855–1898)** — a colliery payroll index that is the most direct finding aid for immigrant miners in this era. ⚠️ **Its repository and access details are unconfirmed** by the tools; you will need to verify the holder directly.

---

### Catholic Church Records
Irish miners were overwhelmingly Catholic. Parish baptismal and marriage registers are held by **dioceses**, not counties, and the diocesan jurisdiction for the coal region shifted over the period:
- **Diocese of Philadelphia** (early period)
- **Diocese of Scranton** (established 1868, covers much of Lackawanna and Luzerne)
- **Diocese of Allentown** / **Diocese of Harrisburg** may cover portions of Carbon and Schuylkill

Locating the specific parish (e.g., St. Patrick's in Pottsville, St. Joseph's in Mahanoy City) is essential before searching registers.

---

### Record Availability Gaps Noted
The survey found that:
- Most FamilySearch **indexed collections** for Pennsylvania are for later years or are not name-searchable for this period
- **Census, land, and newspaper coverage** for the coal region specifically did not surface through the catalog tools
- A Schuylkill church collection was excluded because it was flagged as a test fixture

---

### Recommended Next Steps
1. **Run county-by-county surveys** starting with Schuylkill to find county-level holdings
2. **Search for the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** directly — contact the Lackawanna County Historical Society or the Anthracite Heritage Museum in Scranton
3. **Identify the parish** your ancestors attended (township or borough of residence narrows this considerably)
4. **Check the Bureau of Mines records** — Pennsylvania's mine inspection reports (from 1870 on) list miners by name at some collieries
5. **Naturalization records** in Schuylkill and Luzerne county courts are strong for Irish immigrants of this era

---

*Note: Collection names above come from tool results returned during this session. The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index is named on the FamilySearch Wiki but its availability and holder are unconfirmed by the catalog tools.*

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Pennsylvania Coal Region Records — Overview
The Pennsylvania Coal Region Records page gathers specialized indexes for the anthracite counties (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, Carbon) that sit alongside the standard civil records. It describes colliery employment indexes drawn from company payroll books, coal-region Catholic parish survival, and the triennial state tax assessments — sources unique to the anthracite field. See the full page for the specific index titles and their coverage years.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]

## Pennsylvania Coal Region Records — Choosing an index
Anthracite-region researchers should distinguish company payroll indexes (which name individual colliery workers) from mine-inspection and accident reports (which are organized by colliery, not by person). Payroll-derived indexes are the more direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were indexed inconsistently in census records.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced for Vermont's pre-statehood period (saved as **loc_001** in your project):

---

**Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Guide (c. 1770–1791)**

**Political Background**
Vermont did not become a state until 1791. During the late 1700s the territory was contested between New Hampshire and New York, and from 1777 it operated as the independent Republic of Vermont. This contested status directly shapes what records were created and where they are held.

**Key Record Types and What to Expect**

| Record Type | What Exists | Where to Look |
|---|---|---|
| **Early resident lists** | The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (New Hampshire grantees, prepared under New York colonial authority) is the principal pre-statehood population listing confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki | FamilySearch and state archives |
| **Civil registration** | Statewide civil registration did not begin until **1857** — before then, births, marriages, and deaths survive only unevenly | Town clerk offices (each town kept its own) |
| **Town records** | Vermont towns were incorporated under New Hampshire grants, and many kept early proprietors' records | Vermont State Archives; individual town clerk offices |
| **Land / deeds** | Land grants from both New Hampshire and New York overlap for this period | Town land records; New York State Archives (for NY-era grants) |
| **Church records** | Congregational, Baptist, and other churches kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers | Church archives; local historical societies |
| **Cemetery records** | Many pre-statehood burials are in family or church burying grounds | Local historical societies; FindAGrave; cemetery transcription projects |
| **Probate records** | Probate was handled at the county level after Vermont's county system was established | Vermont county probate courts; Vermont State Archives |
| **Early censuses** | Vermont was not yet a state for the 1790 federal census (it appears as an early 1791 enumeration) | FamilySearch; National Archives |

**Research Gaps and Caveats**
- A search of FamilySearch's digitized collections for Vermont in this period returned no confirmed indexed records, so coverage there is spotty.
- Pre-statehood records are especially fragmented because the competing New Hampshire/New York/Vermont Republic jurisdictions each generated different record sets.
- The FamilySearch Wiki confirms the 1771 survey and the 1857 civil registration start date; other Vermont-specific source details (court, church, early census) remain to be confirmed through catalog searches.

**Recommended Next Steps**
1. Use **research-plan** to convert this guide into a sequenced search plan for a specific ancestor.
2. Run targeted FamilySearch catalog searches for Vermont county and town records.
3. Check the Vermont State Archives directly for pre-1800 town and proprietary records.
4. Search the 1790/1791 federal census for your surnames of interest.

home.content:
# Vermont Genealogy

Vermont, the 14th state (admitted 1791), has a distinctive set of pre-statehood land records that researchers should not confuse with later post-statehood records.

## Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule
The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule, prepared under New York colonial authority before statehood, enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry lists grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This record predates any Vermont civil registration and is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state.

## Civil Vital Records
Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857. Earlier town clerk records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly; consult town clerk offices directly.

## Town Histories
Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860-1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access.

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

home.content:
# Genealogy Research Guide

This jurisdiction has a variety of genealogical records available for researchers. Key record types include:

## Vital Records
Birth, marriage, and death records availability varies by time period. Civil registration dates differ by jurisdiction — check the specific start dates before assuming records exist.

## Census Records
Federal census records are available from 1790 (with gaps). State and territorial censuses may fill gaps between federal enumerations.

## Church Records
Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate civil registration and may be the only source for vital events in earlier periods. Check both the denomination's archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

## Land Records
Land grants, deeds, and patents are held at county courthouses, state archives, and (for federal land states) the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website.

## Probate Records
Wills, inventories, and administration records are typically held at the county courthouse or state archives.

## Court Records
Court files include naturalizations, guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases that may name family members.

## Military Records
Service records, pension files, and draft registrations are at the National Archives. State adjutant general records may be at the state archives.

## Immigration and Naturalization
Passenger lists are at NARA. Naturalization records are scattered across federal, state, and local courts (pre-1906).

question.content:
## Research Guidance — Record Types
Genealogical research for this locality and period draws on several record classes. Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) may begin late — many jurisdictions did not require civil registration until the late 1800s or early 1900s, so earlier events are documented in church registers, family bibles, and cemetery records. Census records, land and property records, probate files, court records, and newspapers fill the gaps. Check the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific county or town to see which collections have been microfilmed or digitized.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance]

## Research Guidance — Repositories
Records are held across multiple repositories: the county courthouse (deeds, probate, court, marriage), the state archives (vital records, state censuses, military), denominational archives (church registers), and the National Archives (federal census, military service and pension files, naturalizations, passenger lists). Local historical and genealogical societies often hold transcriptions, cemetery surveys, and manuscript collections not available elsewhere.
[https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Research_Guidance#Repositories]

vitalRecords.content:
# England Civil Registration

Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths in England and Wales began on **1 July 1837**. Before this date, no civil birth certificates exist — the primary sources for births before 1837 are Anglican parish registers recording baptisms.

## Registration Start Date

The Registration Act 1836 established the system of civil registration that came into force on 1 July 1837. The General Register Office (GRO) was established to oversee registration.

## Before Civil Registration (before 1 July 1837)

For events before 1837, the main alternatives are:

- **Anglican parish registers** — recording baptisms (not births), marriages, and burials. The oldest date from the 1530s.
- **Bishop's transcripts** — annual copies of parish registers sent to the diocesan bishop, often surviving where original registers do not.
- **Nonconformist records** — Baptists, Methodists, Quakers, and other dissenting congregations kept their own registers. Many were deposited at the General Register Office in 1837 and are now at the National Archives (RG 4–8).

## Early Registration (1837–1875)

Early civil registration was incomplete. The requirement to register was established in law, but enforcement was weak in the early years. Many births, deaths, and marriages were never registered. Parish records remain essential even after 1837 for this reason.

## Finding Civil Registration Records

Civil registration indexes (organized quarterly from 1837) are the finding aid for GRO records. Indexes are available at:
- **FreeBMD** (free, volunteer-transcribed)
- **Findmypast** (subscription)
- **Ancestry** (subscription)
- **GRO Historical Indexes** (gov.uk, free for births and deaths 1837–1957)
